column4: Zaqqum is introduced as food in the punishment scene, a specific parallel to the section's thorny, unsatisfying food.
This verse identifies Zaqqum as the sinner's food, directly extending the section's scene of food that cannot nourish.
The punishment's Zaqqum fruit is like molten metal boiling in bellies, intensifying the section's fiery food-and-drink image.
This completes the boiling image with a comparison to boiling water, parallel to the section's scalding drink.
The sinner is seized and dragged to the middle of the Fire, continuing the section's forced punishment scene.
Boiling water is poured over the sinner's head, a direct counterpart to the section's hot spring and fire.
This verse gives the left-hand group's food as Zaqqum, a parallel to the section's thorny food in Hell.
They fill their bellies with that tree's fruit, sharpening the contrast with the section's food that cannot satisfy hunger.
They drink boiling water after the tree's fruit, joining the section's unsatisfying food and scalding drink.
The drinkers gulp like thirsty camels, joining the section's singled-out camel with its contrast between easy milk and tormenting drink.
The verse calls this their welcome on the Day of Judgment, turning garden hospitality into punishment.
This verse answers 18:29's scalding drink with gardens, couches, silk, and ornaments, furnishing the garden counterpart developed in the section.
The couches are lined with brocade and their fruit is near, adding textile and provision details to the section's furnished garden room.
The garden's couches are richly woven, a direct furnishing parallel to the section's raised seats and arranged pillows.
The residents recline face to face on those couches, adding a specific posture to the section's furnished garden scene.
Gold platters and cups circulate in the garden, a specific parallel to the section's cups set out among its furnishings.
This verse commands looking at fruit as it forms and ripens, joining the section's gaze at created earth to food growing from it.
The heavens are raised without visible pillars, repeating the section's invitation to look at how the sky was raised.
The earth is spread with mountains, rivers, and varied growth, echoing the section's sequence of sky, mountain, and earth.
The verse joins unsupported heavens, mountains, animals, and rain-grown plants, extending the section's look from landscape to living provision.
Firm mountains and paths are set on earth here, a specific parallel to the section's mountains erected and earth spread.
Livestock are created for warmth and practical benefits, specifying the usefulness behind the section's invitation to look at the camel.
The herds are beautiful when brought back in the evening and sent out in the morning, echoing the section's day's walk and evening return around the camel image.
Livestock carry people and their burdens to distant lands, giving concrete travel use to the camel that opens the section's visual inquiry.
Livestock provide drink from their bellies and food, closely joining the section's camel scene to the milk passed easily to drinkers.
People are carried on livestock and ships, extending the section's camel from a created sign to a means of travel.
Created livestock are placed in human possession, paralleling the section's question about how the camel was created for use.
The livestock are made subject to people for riding and food, linking the section's camel and provisions.
Livestock yield benefits and drink, a direct parallel to the section's animal-derived furnishing and milk scenes.
The food inspection of 80:24 continues with grain grown from the split earth, identifying what that looking reveals.
This continuation names grapes and fodder, linking the earth's growth to food for people and animals.
Olives and date palms continue the food inventory that follows the section's call to inspect one's food.
Dense gardens extend the food-and-earth scene after 80:24's invitation to look at food.
Fruit and pasture continue the provision scene, joining the section's garden food to the camel's earthly nourishment.
The produce is provision for people and livestock, completing the food list that links the section's camel, earth, and eating.
Dead earth revived with grain for eating joins the section's soil-to-resurrection proof to its questions about food and creation.
Gardens of palms and vines with springs extend the same earth-revival sign into garden provision, matching the section's flowing spring and fruit.
The fruit is food from gardens people did not make, a specific reminder that the section's garden provisions are created and provided.
This verse says no small or great deed is omitted from the opened record, repeating the section's link between its account and what is written.
Two recorders sit on the right and left, giving a concrete account-keeping scene behind the section's claim that the Messenger is not the keeper.
No word is spoken without a watcher ready to record it, joining the section's silence about idle speech to its reckoning and record.
Every atom's weight of good will be seen, specifying the small-scale measure behind the section's work and final account.
Every atom's weight of evil will likewise be seen, completing the section's account of both outcomes.
Scales of justice are set on the Day and no soul is wronged even by a mustard seed, making the section's account a precise measure.
The section names the ح س ب root in its sufficiency sense; this verse says “Allah is sufficient for us,” alongside reliance on Him.
The same root's sufficiency sense appears in “Allah is sufficient for you,” distinct from its accounting use in the section's final verse.
The Messenger says “Allah is sufficient for me,” a further Quranic use of the section's named root in its sufficiency sense.
Every soul is returned to God and confronted with what it did, directly joining the section's return to its accounting.
People return to God and are told what they did, echoing the section's pairing of return with account.
All return to their Lord, who informs them of their deeds, matching the section's sequence of return and reckoning.
The peaceful soul offers another face of the section's satisfied outcome before its return to God and entry into the garden.
The soul is told to return to its Lord pleased and pleasing, a direct parallel to the section's satisfied face and final return.
The returning soul is welcomed among God's servants, completing 89:28's return as a communal garden entry beside the section's garden gathering.
The returned soul is told to enter Paradise, completing the section's link between return and the high garden.
The section's mountain image meets its secondary return root here: mountains are commanded to join David in praise, using the A-W-B root.
This verse calls the repentant “awwābīn”; it is another use of the section's word for a person who turns back to God.
Faces on that Day are divided between brightness and darkness, repeating the section's paired faces and their opposed outcomes.
The bright-faced group is in God's mercy, specifying the garden side of the section's two faces on that Day.
Those who do good receive more and have no dust or humiliation on their faces, a specific reversal of the section's punished faces.
Mountains are moved away on the Hour, reversing the section's view of them firmly set in the created landscape.
A pregnant she-camel is abandoned when the Hour arrives; this is a specific inversion of the section's useful, observed camel, though the link is distant.
Earth and mountains are lifted and crushed on the Day, reversing the section's spread earth and erected mountains.
The sky splits on that Day, a specific reversal of the section's raised and constructed heaven.
Mountains are moved and earth exposed on the gathering Day, undoing the formed landscape the section asks the eye to inspect.
The question about what happens to mountains on the Day returns to the section's question of how they were set up.
The mountains are crushed to dust, a direct reversal of their firm erection in the section's creation scene.
The land is left level, with no crookedness or unevenness, reversing the section's spread earth as a prepared surface.
